ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a casual, collegial video-call style, with mostly short-to-medium turns in the opening and Q&A but long, structured monologue turns during presentations. Overlap is occasional, especially in greetings, transitions, and follow-up questions, though participants generally wait for answers rather than aggressively interrupting. Speech is informal and highly disfluent: frequent “um,” “yeah,” “okay,” repetitions, restarts, self-corrections, and unfinished clauses are common, particularly among speakers formulating technical questions in real time. Participants hedge often with phrases like “I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” “I guess,” “it seems,” and “I’m not sure,” while speakers answer cautiously and acknowledge uncertainty directly. The tone is friendly and supportive, with praise before questions and disagreement or correction framed indirectly through curiosity, caveats, or alternative possibilities. Questions are typically prefaced as “quick,” “naive,” or “good” questions, then unfold into multipart, exploratory prompts; answers are expansive, conversational, and often end by naming open questions rather than claiming certainty.

Meeting style for this meeting (quick_checkin): A rushed weekly check-in. People give short status updates and ask each other quick questions. Most turns are one or two sentences. Nobody summarizes. Someone has another meeting soon and the conversation stops where it stops.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - Okay, so, quick one from me- the export finished last night, mostly.
  - Mostly?
  - Two of the sites didn't come through. I haven't looked yet.
Opening: Start with a person asking for a quick catch-up because they missed the last meeting.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Setting up wastewater monitoring for infectious disease in a mid-sized city and deciding who sees the data.

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Chen
speakers.background: A fifth-year doctoral candidate embedded with Riverton's public-health department, Chen has spent four years analyzing respiratory-virus surveillance data, including syndromic indicators, laboratory reporting delays, and wastewater-to-clinical lead-lag models. She is experienced with RT-qPCR-derived viral concentration data and routinely translates statistical outputs into short technical briefs for communicable-disease staff.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Chen treats wastewater as a population-level early indicator rather than a measure of individual infections. She focuses on denominator problems, reporting lags, assay comparability, temporal trends, and conservative threshold interpretation. In the pilot, she is likely to press for clearly defined baseline periods, confidence-aware language, and documentation that signals can precede reported clinical cases by roughly 5-10 days without being convertible into case counts.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Prof. Elena Ruiz
speakers.background: Ruiz is a principal investigator with 12 years of research on public-health data infrastructures, environmental sensing, and civic participation. Her work combines interviews, document analysis, meeting observation, and participatory design workshops with communities and public agencies. She has studied how dashboards, maps, and uncertainty statements shape who can interpret a public-health signal and whose concerns are treated as credible.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Ruiz approaches wastewater surveillance as a sociotechnical system rather than a neutral measurement pipeline. She is attentive to how sewershed boundaries become public categories, how restricted and public-facing dashboards distribute interpretive authority, and whether uncertainty is made legible rather than buried in technical caveats. She will ask which institutional actors can validate a public signal, what residents are expected to infer from delayed citywide summaries, and how the project can earn trust without implying precision it does not possess.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Alex Morgan
speakers.background: Morgan is a postdoctoral researcher in urban water systems engineering with six years of field and laboratory experience in wastewater-based epidemiology. They have designed autosampler deployments, delineated collection-system catchments using GIS and hydraulic records, and evaluated flow normalization, precipitation effects, sample preservation, and site-access constraints across municipal utilities. Morgan has worked directly with plant operators and understands the practical limits of upstream monitoring.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Morgan frames the pilot around representativeness and measurement integrity: whether a sampling point has a stable contributing population, whether a 24-hour composite can be collected reliably, and whether observed concentration changes reflect pathogen shedding rather than hydraulic dilution or industrial and stormwater inputs. They favor treatment-plant influent for stable aggregate trends while recognizing that upstream manholes can provide more localized information at the cost of smaller, volatile catchments. Morgan is likely to challenge proposals that treat administrative neighborhoods or dashboard categories as equivalent to hydraulically defensible sewersheds.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely

transcript.speaker: Alex Morgan
transcript.text: Hi, sorry, I missed the end of the last discussion—did we settle on the two plants as the baseline sites, or are the upstream locations still co-equal options? I was hoping we could get clear today on what the utility can actually support for twice-weekly 24-hour composites before we turn the site list into the pilot design.

transcript.speaker: Prof. Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: Mm, still open, I think.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I'd keep the two plants as the baseline sites, at least for the first six months. They give us a citywide signal we can interpret without- we don't want to accidentally treat an upstream blip like a neighborhood outbreak. The upstream sites could be a smaller add-on if the composite sampling capacity is there.

transcript.speaker: Alex Morgan
transcript.text: I'd set both influents as the fixed sites for twice-weekly, 24-hour composites. Then any upstream work is conditional on a real site check for power, a safe sampler footprint, and a catchment we can actually delineate. I'm least ready to promise the university manhole until we check the dry-weather flow and access.

transcript.speaker: Prof. Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: That conditional framing matters, especially for how we explain it publicly. Alex, when you do the delineation, are those residential catchments hydraulically coherent enough that a resident wouldn’t read the label as a regular—an ordinary neighborhood boundary? I’ve seen people accept uncertainty in timing, but react pretty strongly when the infrastructure category turns out not to match the place name.

transcript.speaker: Alex Morgan
transcript.text: Probably not, no. The residential sewersheds may be hydraulically coherent, but the contributing areas can cross those street-level neighborhood labels, and there may be institutional or commercial parcels in there too. I'd give a plain-language catchment description and a map, with the caveat that it's a flow-contribution area, not a community boundary. I need to verify the actual delineations against the utility's records first, and then...

transcript.speaker: Prof. Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: That’s exactly the distinction I’d want out in the open, not tucked away in metadata. A map could still be useful internally, but for anything public, I’d avoid neighborhood-like labels unless the catchment and the lived geography genuinely line up. Otherwise, people will quite reasonably infer a claim we aren’t making.

transcript.speaker: Alex Morgan
transcript.text: And even internally, I’d keep the GIS polygon tied to a versioned hydraulic delineation, because a diversion or a service change can alter it. I’ll ask the utility whether any of the residential areas have known, known industrial discharges or wet-weather inflow issues before we rank them as upstream candidates.

transcript.speaker: Prof. Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: Hm, worth checking.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: The wet-weather piece matters for interpretation at the plants too. Alex, do your flow records suggest normalization stays reasonably comparable during rain events, or would we need to flag, flag those samples instead of reading a concentration change as a transmission signal?

transcript.speaker: Alex Morgan
transcript.text: I'd flag rain-affected upstream samples by default. At the plants, flow-normalizing the RT-qPCR concentrations should make the series more comparable, but it doesn't magically remove every wet-weather effect. I've seen targets and fecal markers decouple during moderate storms, so I'd keep the raw concentration, flow, and rainfall fields and interpret a spike cautiously rather than automatically excluding...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That works for me. I’d build a rain flag into the dashboard and treat those observations as qualified, not threshold-triggering on their own. The useful lead is usually only about five to ten days ahead of reported cases, so we don’t need to overreact to a single, single noisy point. We should make that interpretation rule explicit for the 15 May submission.

transcript.speaker: Prof. Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: And could we put that qualification in the public summary too, not just the technical dashboard? Otherwise, a citywide line is going to look much more settled than it- than it really is. Maya, what would make you move from calling it ordinary variation to calling it a meaningful increase, two aligned samples or something else?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I’d want two consecutive samples moving in the same direction before we call it an increase, ideally with both the normalized concentration and a fecal marker behaving normally. A single high point, especially with rain, would be a result to watch, not an alert. Then we can say the signal may precede reported clinical data by roughly five to ten days, not that it predicts case numbers.

transcript.speaker: Prof. Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: Yeah, two samples feels important.

transcript.speaker: Alex Morgan
transcript.text: And I’d add that “fecal marker behaving normally” needs to be a review criterion, not a hard correction factor. At the plant sites, we can usually look at it alongside flow and rainfall. Upstream, if the marker and target decouple, I’d rather label that sample indeterminate until we know if it’s an inflow issue or a composite-collection issue.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Agreed, it’s a review criterion, not a formula. For the protocol, I’ll make indeterminate a real category alongside ordinary variation and a sustained increase, so a decoupled upstream result doesn’t turn into an alert just because it’s high.

transcript.speaker: Alex Morgan
transcript.text: I’d also make the indeterminate category available at the plant sites if we lose a flow record or the composite log shows a collection failure. Volume-normalized concentration is still useful, but I wouldn’t want to- I wouldn’t want missing hydraulics quietly treated as comparable data. Maya, would you still use that as supporting context, just not for the sustained-increase call?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Exactly, keep it as context, but it can’t contribute to the sustained-increase call if the flow record or composite collection is compromised. We can still note it internally and see whether the next valid sample corroborates it. With only a roughly five-to-ten-day lead over reported cases, waiting for that second sound point is still useful.

transcript.speaker: Prof. Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: That also makes the public-language question a little clearer. We should distinguish “no clear interpretation” from “no signal,” because otherwise people will read an indeterminate point as reassurance. I’ll draft that uncertainty note, though I need to check whether the city’s public-data policy triggers an accessibility or language review for the summary.

transcript.speaker: Alex Morgan
transcript.text: Yeah, and I’ll confirm the site-access constraints before we lock any upstream language.

transcript.speaker: Prof. Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: And I’ll make that access distinction explicit too. The health department can see the qualified site-level evidence, but the public summary is a delayed citywide trend, not a neighborhood diagnosis. That should keep the one-week delay from looking arbitrary or, worse, like we’re withholding some precise local finding...

transcript.speaker: Alex Morgan
transcript.text: Mm, that distinction helps.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: For the health department dashboard, I'd keep the site-level traces visible, along with the rain, flow, and collection qualifiers. But I'd frame the whole thing as an early population signal, usually about five to ten days ahead of complete clinical reporting, not a local case estimate. I still need the lab to confirm that influenza, COVID, and norovirus can all stay on that twice-weekly cadence within budget.

transcript.speaker: Alex Morgan
transcript.text: For the lab confirmation, one practical thing is that the plant composite volumes and the preservation window matter as much as the assay list. If they can handle twice-weekly influenza, SARS-CoV-2, and norovirus, I’ll make sure we ask if they need a fixed pickup cutoff, because otherwise a 24-hour composite can end up with a pretty variable hold time before extraction.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That pickup cutoff should go into the lab question, plus the actual turnaround from receipt to result. If a Tuesday composite isn’t extracted until Friday, the nominal five-to-ten-day lead gets eaten up pretty, pretty quickly. I’d rather know the hold-time limits before we call twice weekly workable.

transcript.speaker: Prof. Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: Hm, timing could be tight.

transcript.speaker: Alex Morgan
transcript.text: For the collection side, I’d want the lab to state the maximum time from the end of the composite to extraction, not just pickup, and whether chilled storage preserves all three targets over that window. If their turnaround is too variable, we may need to stagger the two plant composites instead of assuming both can close on the same morning.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: If we stagger them, I’d just want the schedule fixed enough that we can still assess two consecutive valid samples consistently. Otherwise that five-to-ten-day early window gets pretty thin. And the lab needs to tell us whether that preservation window is the same for all three targets. I don’t know that it...

transcript.speaker: Alex Morgan
transcript.text: Yeah—let’s not assume the preservation window is uniform across targets.

transcript.speaker: Prof. Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: Okay, I think we can stop there and give everyone a few minutes back. Thanks, both. I'll see you next week—

transcript.speaker: Alex Morgan
transcript.text: All right, take care.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Bye, both.
